Witch flounder (Glyptocephalus cynoglossus) exhibits a characteristic life history pattern for a deepwater pleuronectiform, with females attaining a maximum recorded body length of 60 cm [Li = 60 cm]. Field surveys of the Grand Banks stock indicate that the total length at which 50% of individuals reach puberty is 30.4 cm [Lp = 30.4 cm], a value consistent with the size structure of spawning aggregations in the Gulf of St. Lawrence. The wet weight of newly hatched larvae, based on the average egg diameter of 1.16 mm, is approximately 0.00055 g [Wwb = approximately 0.00055 g], reflecting the extremely small propagule size typical of species with a prolonged pelagic larval duration. This modest initial mass contrasts sharply with the ultimate female wet weight, which has been estimated at 1,500 g [Wwi = 1,500 g] using length-weight relationships derived from commercial trawl catches, underscoring the considerable scope for somatic growth over the lifespan.

Reproductive output in this species has been evaluated under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable temperature of 6 °C [T = 6 °C], reflecting the thermal regime of its primary deepwater habitat. At a body length of 26.8 cm, which is below the size at puberty, females nonetheless produce an estimated 134 eggs per day  when the daily rate is averaged over the spawning season at a temperature of 6 °C [T = 6 °C]. By contrast, at a length of 42 cm, the annual fecundity increases dramatically to approximately 599,000 eggs per year , a value that integrates both the higher batch fecundity and the extended spawning frequency of larg at a temperature of 6 °C [T = 6 °C]er individuals. This marked size-dependent increase in reproductive output, recorded at the same thermal regime of 6 °C, highlights the strong selective advantage of large body size in this species.

Egg development and the timing of hatching are highly dependent on ambient temperature in the early life stages. At an incubation temperature of 8.6 °C [T = 8.6 °C], the interval from fertilization to hatching is approximately 8 days [ab = approximately 8 days], a relatively short duration that reflects the elevated metabolic rates characteristic of warmer incubation conditions. The freshly hatched yolk-sac larva weighs just 0.00055 g [Wwb = 0.00055 g], a figure supported by volumetric calculations from the spherical egg diameter, and carries an endogenous yolk reserve that sustains it through the lecithotrophic phase until the onset of first exogenous feeding. The rapid progression from embryonated egg to free-swimming larva under these thermal conditions is an adaptation to reduce predation risk during the vulnerable pre-feeding interval.

The wet weight at puberty for female Witch flounder is 167 g [Wwp = 167 g], derived from the length-weight relationship using the total length at puberty of 30.4 cm [Lp = 30.4 cm]. This mass threshold marks the transition from the immature juvenile stage to reproductive competence, and it represents a body size approximately one-ninth of the ultimate female wet weight of 1,500 g [Wwi = 1,500 g]. The substantial growth increment between puberty and maximum size indicates that most reproductive output is contributed by larger, older females. Field observations from the Newfoundland slope confirm that puberty is attained at a total length of 30.4 cm [Lp = 30.4 cm], corresponding to an estimated age of 4-5 years under typical growth conditions in the cold northwest Atlantic.

Longevity records for this species indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 9,125 days [am = approximately 9,125 days] when maintained at 6 °C [T = 6 °C], a duration that places this species among the longer-lived pleuronectiforms. In larger individuals exceeding 42 cm in total length, the estimated annual reproductive output amounts to approximately 599,000 oocytes , a value that underscores the contribution of size to lifetime fecundity. The maximum total length of 60 cm [Li = 60 cm] is rarely attained, as most individuals in surveyed populations measure between 35 and 50 cm. Nonetheless, the combination of delayed puberty at 167 g [Wwp = 167 g] and substantial longevity allows for a lifetime reproductive output that may exceed several million eggs per female under favorable conditions in the stable deepwater environment at 6 °C.
